We refer to this as the Graph Degree Task. LLMs follow a sequential randomized process to generate their outputs. As a result, their inputs are received and processed as ordered sequences. In particular, when the input is lengthy, LLMs are known to pay “less attention” to certain regions of the input, hence, struggling with retaining information from those regions. This leads to a performance degradation over extended inputs [ 23]. For example, Fig 1 shows the significant error of GPT-3.5 Turbo for Graph Degree Task when the graph size is more than 200. On the other hand, the input of a symmetric task is an unordered bag of elements. As a result, the input elements can be freely re- ordered. This gives us the opportunity to rerank the input elements before passing it to the LLM for maximizing its accuracy – which is the research focus of this paper. Specifically, we introduce a rerank- ing mechanism that (a) learns the so-called “exposure” of each rank position for an LLM during the preprocessing time. Then, at the query time, it (b) assesses the relevance of each input element to the given natural language query and (c) generates a reranking of the input that puts the relevant elements in high-exposure positions.

Additionally, we conducted experiments on other tasks, such as database query answering with real-world datasets, and observed comparable improvements in the output of the LLMs after reranking the input. More details on the experiments and more empirical results are provided in the Technical Report [9].

Based on Figure 3, GPT-3.5 Turbo tends to focus more on the beginning of a long prompt, while it is more likely to forget the later tokens. In contrast, GPT-4o Mini shows a different pattern, where it is more likely to forget tokens at the start and the end while keeping those in the middle. As shown in the Technical Report [ 9], Phi-4 behaves similarly to GPT-4o Mini, mainly retaining the middle part of the prompt. On the other hand, Gemma-2 remembers tokens at the end of the prompt but tends to forget the beginning. We leverage the exposures identified in this subsection as a preprocessing step to address the subsequent tasks discussed in the following subsection.

In this section, we present a detailed overview of the task setups and the datasets utilized. theDBLP ACM dataset [ 29], with approximately 132,000 entries. This dataset provides a comprehensive list of research papers, including attributes such as titles, authors, and the journals in which the papers were published. It is widely used for entity resolution tasks. For our study, we extracted a smaller sample of rows from this dataset. The task involved passing the sampled DataFrame to the LLM as input and querying it with questions such as, "How many papers were published in physics-related journals?" to determine the number of papers relevant to a given research topic. using the Erdős-Rényi model [ 14], where the edges represent the set of elements, denoted as I. The primary query qfor this graph is: “What is the degree of a given node v?”. We systematically select various nodes vwithin the graph and evaluate the responses provided by an LLM to these queries. Since the generated graph is fully accessible, we can compute the ground-truth degree of eachqueried node. To assess the accuracy of the LLM’s responses, we calculate the error εLas the absolute difference between the degree reported by the LLM and the ground-truth degree. We first pass the set of edges to the LLM and then ask the query in a different prompt message but in the same context. We selected graph sizes up to 500 edges to generate synthetic graphs to ensure that all edges could be represented within a single prompt when inputting them into LLMs, thereby adhering to the models’ token limits. in this task, we provide a dataset table as input to the LLM and ask aggregation queries in natural language. For instance, a query might ask, "How many rows contain the value in the ‘col’ column equal to ‘value’?" We utilize three real-world datasets for this study. The IMDB Movies dataset[ 26] provides information on the top 1,000 movies listed on IMDB . We extract a subset containing 60 rows from this dataset and formulate a query regarding the number of movies with a rating ofRating≥8.2. TheAdult Income dataset [ 2], which comprises data on approximately 48,000 individuals for income prediction tasks, is also employed. From this dataset, we sample 60 rows and pose a query about the number of individuals associated with a specific “workclass” category. Finally, the Open University Learning Analytics ( OULAD ) dataset [ 19] includes data on student enrollments across various courses. It contains 32K rows. For our task, we sample a subset of 100 rows and ask about the number of students enrolled in a particular course. These sample sizes are carefully selected to align with the token limits of LLMs4. The re- sults for the Adults and OULAD are presented in the Technical Report [9].

In this subsection, we utilize different small-sizes open-source LLMs as helpers (H) to estimate the relevance scores of elements to the query (Relq). We use five different models: DeepSeek-Coder- v2:16B [43],Gemma2:9B [36],Llama3.1:8B [11],Qwen2:7B [41], andMistral:7B [18]. This selection, while random within the range of small models (approximately 7B–8B parameters), ensures cover- age of diverse and widely used open-source models. We compare four ranking methods in this experiment. The first method, Warm-up, as described in Section 3.1, involves querying each partition of the input and subsequently splitting it. The second method, Bipartite, detailed in Section 3.2, utilizes Bipartite Graph Modeling to estimate relevance scores. To establish a lower bound for performance comparison, we use the Random method, which involves randomly shuffling all the input elements within the set I and passing them to the language model, L. We expect this method to give us less accurate results. As an upper bound, we employ the Optimum method, where elements are completely sorted based on explicit knowledge of the task to maximize relevance to the query. This approach provides a theoretical upper limit for ranking utility, and we expect it to give us the best answer. For example, for the 4GPT-3.5-Turbo has a token limit of 4,096. For this model, we selected 60 rows from the ADULT dataset, which resulted in almost 3,244 tokens. For GPT-4o-mini, which supports a significantly larger context window of 128k tokens, we selected a corre- spondingly larger number of rows.

Table 1 presents the comparison of ranking utilities across dif- ferent models and methods (more results on additional datasets are illustrated in the Technical Report [ 9]). The Random and Optimum methods serve as lower and upper bounds, respectively, providing benchmarks for comparison independent of any specific helper model. Due to the variability introduced by sampling, slight dif- ferences in the ranking utilities across different models can occurfor these two methods, even though they do not use any helper models.
